newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO chief urges Croatia to honour peace accords.
newsitem.headline: NATO chief urges Croatia to honour peace accords.

text.p: NATO urged Croatia on Tuesday to stick to commitments made under peace accords which ended the Balkan conflicts if it wishes to win more acceptance in the West, alliance officials said.
They said NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana told Croatian Prime Minister Zlatko Metesa his country must continue to show its support for the Dayton peace deal.
"The secretary-general was very forceful and underlined his concern in a number of areas. He accepted there had been progress, but the message was: no backsliding," one official said.

NATO has been concerned by recent attempts by the Croatian authorities to make the alliance pay for flights over Croatian airspace and for the use of its ports by troops serving in the peacekeeping mission in Bosnia.
Before the alliance-led mission entered Bosnia to oversee implementation of the Dayton accords, NATO signed a status of force agreement with Croatia which allowed it free use of such facilities.
Implementation Force (IFOR) troops are also exempted from Croatian tax and can cross the border with Bosnia at will.
"There have been a number of border incidents where IFOR troops have even been fired on by border guards," the official said. "We want to see an end to such things."

Matesa said the two men discussed the Bosnian city of Mostar, divided between Moslems and Bosnian Croats, but said that tensions over Zagreb's role in failing to control Croat nationalists was "now a thing of the past".
He added that the government of President Franjo Tudjman was committed to the Dayton accords which last year ended the 3 1/2- year Bosnian war, and to rebuilding regional stability.
"Dayton has to work because there is no other reasonable solution," he told Reuters.

Metesa was in Brussels with Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic for talks with NATO and the European Union and to inaugurate a two-day trade fair designed to attract investment and help change the country's image as a zone of conflict.

On Monday, EU External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek met the two men and said the EU would review its position on frozen negotiations over a lucrative trade and cooperation deal towards the end of the year.

Both NATO and EU officials stressed further progress on establishing close links with Croatia would depend on how Zagreb worked to make the Moslem-Croat Federation in Bosnia, a cornerstone of Dayton, a reality.
